example_en: I have my own room.
notes: Cambridge Learner's Dictionary classifies own as adjective, pronoun and determiner at A2 and gives UK pronunciation /əʊn/. In 'my own room', own functions adjectivally and means belonging to the speaker. Example and Ukrainian translation match.

example_en: There is a painting on the wall.
notes: Cambridge Dictionary explicitly labels the countable picture sense A2 and gives UK IPA /ˈpeɪn.tɪŋ/. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the countable picture sense.

example_en: She has the ability to learn quickly.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists ability n. at A2. Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary gives UK IPA /əˈbɪləti/ and defines the noun as the fact of being able to do something or a level of skill. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the ability-to-do-something sense.

example_en: I was able to finish the task on time.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists able adj. at A2. Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary gives UK IPA /ˈeɪbl/ and the pattern 'be able to do something'. The example correctly uses 'was able to' followed by the infinitive; the Ukrainian translation preserves the successful-completion meaning.

example_en: My brother works abroad.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists abroad adv. at A2. Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary gives UK IPA /əˈbrɔːd/ and the sense 'in or to a foreign country'. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the location use.

example_en: She decided to accept the job offer.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists accept v. at A2. Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary gives UK IPA /əkˈsept/ and the sense of willingly taking something offered. The example uses the natural collocation 'accept a job offer'; the Ukrainian translation is accurate.

example_en: The accident happened near the station.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists accident n. at A2. Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary gives UK IPA /ˈæksɪdənt/ and the countable sense of an unexpected unpleasant event, especially one causing injury or damage. The example and Ukrainian translation match this sense.

example_en: He worked hard to achieve his goal.
example_uk: Він наполегливо працював, щоб досягти своєї мети.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists achieve v. at A2. Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary gives UK IPA /əˈtʃiːv/ and the sense of succeeding in reaching a goal or standard, especially through effort. The example and Ukrainian translation match this sense.

example_en: We need to act quickly.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists act v. at A2 (the noun is separately listed at B1). Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary gives UK IPA /ækt/ and includes the verb sense 'do something for a particular purpose or to deal with a situation'. The example and Ukrainian translation match the verb use.

example_en: My grandfather is still active.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists active adj. at A2. Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary gives UK IPA /ˈæktɪv/ and the sense 'always busy doing things, especially physical activities'. Cambridge Learner's Dictionary labels a closely corresponding busy sense B1; the project follows its stated Oxford-first CEFR policy and records this source difference.

example_en: Actually, I don't live in London.
example_uk: Насправді я не живу в Лондоні.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists actually adv. at A2. Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary gives UK IPA /ˈæktʃuəli/ and describes its use to emphasize what is really true or to correct a mistaken belief. The sentence and Ukrainian translation illustrate a natural correction/clarification. Note: actually does not mean 'currently'.

example_en: The college offers adult education.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists adult adj. at A2, while adult n. is A1 and is a separate entry/use. Cambridge Learner's Dictionary confirms the adjective sense 'for or relating to adults' at A2 and UK pronunciations /ˈædʌlt, əˈdʌlt/. The example uses the established collocation 'adult education'; the Ukrainian translation is accurate.

example_en: One advantage of this phone is its long battery life.
example_uk: Одна з переваг цього телефона — тривалий час роботи акумулятора.
notes: Oxford 3000 classifies advantage n. as A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ədˈvɑːn.tɪdʒ/ and the noun sense of a condition that gives a greater chance of success, but labels this sense B1; the project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. Original example and Ukrainian translation illustrate a benefit.

example_en: Their trip to Scotland was a real adventure.
example_uk: Їхня подорож до Шотландії стала справжньою пригодою.
notes: Oxford 3000 classifies adventure n. as A2. Cambridge confirms the UK pronunciation /ədˈven.tʃə(r)/ and the countable/uncountable noun sense of an unusual, exciting and possibly dangerous activity or experience. The project's broad non-rhotic IPA omits optional post-vocalic /r/. Example and Ukrainian translation match.

example_en: The company will advertise its new product online.
example_uk: Компанія рекламуватиме свій новий продукт в інтернеті.
notes: Oxford 3000 classifies advertise v. as A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈæd.və.taɪz/; Cambridge's general dictionary labels the core 'make something known to sell it' sense B1. The project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the commercial sense.

example_en: I saw an advertisement for a part-time job.
example_uk: Я побачив оголошення про роботу на неповний робочий день.
notes: Oxford 3000 classifies advertisement n. as A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ədˈvɜː.tɪs.mənt/ and labels the countable noun A2; it also notes the informal British forms 'advert' and 'ad'. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate a job advertisement.

example_en: She works in advertising.
notes: Oxford 3000 classifies advertising n. as A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈæd.və.taɪ.zɪŋ/ and the uncountable noun meaning the business or activity of promoting products or services, but labels this sense B2. The project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example and Ukrainian translation are natural.

example_en: Lack of sleep can affect your concentration.
example_uk: Брак сну може впливати на твою концентрацію.
notes: Oxford 3000 classifies affect v. as A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈfekt/ and the verb meaning 'to influence or cause a change', but labels the main sense B2. The project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. This row is the ordinary verb, not the specialised psychology noun /ˈæfekt/. Example and Ukrainian translation match.

example_en: I'll call you after I get home.
example_uk: Я зателефоную тобі після того, як повернуся додому.
notes: Oxford 3000 lists after as a conjunction at A2 (its preposition use is A1). Cambridge British Grammar confirms that after introduces a clause and that the present simple is used after it for future time. Cambridge UK pronunciation is /ˈɑːf.tə(r)/, represented in broad non-rhotic IPA as /ˈɑːftə/. The example follows the future-time rule.

example_en: I went to the supermarket and met a friend soon after.
example_uk: Я пішов до супермаркету й невдовзі після цього зустрів друга.
notes: Oxford 3000 lists after as an adverb at A2 (its preposition use is A1). Cambridge British Grammar confirms adverbial use, noting that 'afterwards' is more common and that after often occurs in adverb phrases. Cambridge UK pronunciation is /ˈɑːf.tə(r)/, represented in broad non-rhotic IPA as /ˈɑːftə/. Example and Ukrainian translation match the adverbial time meaning.

example_en: She leaned against the wall.
notes: Oxford 3000 classifies against prep. as A2. Cambridge confirms UK variants /əˈɡenst/ and /əˈɡeɪnst/ and labels the physical-contact sense A2. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate physical contact/support. Other senses include opposition and competition.

example_en: Ah, now I understand.
notes: Oxford 3000 classifies ah exclamation as A2. Cambridge Learner's Dictionary confirms UK /ɑː/ and uses of ah to express understanding, sympathy or pleasure. The example illustrates sudden understanding; Ukrainian 'Ага' is natural in this context.

example_en: Which airline are you flying with?
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists airline n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /ˈeəlaɪn/ and defines the noun as a company operating regular passenger or goods flights. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the company sense.

example_en: The fish is still alive.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists alive adj. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /əˈlaɪv/ and the basic meaning 'living; not dead'. The example and Ukrainian translation match this sense.

example_en: The cake was all eaten.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists all adv. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /ɔːl/ and the A2 adverbial meaning 'completely'. The example illustrates the adverb modifying the passive verb phrase.

example_en: Are you all right?
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level includes all right at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /ˌɔːl ˈraɪt/ and its adjective, adverb and discourse-marker uses. The example uses the adjective meaning 'well or safe'. The standard spelling is two words; 'alright' is less standard.

example_en: My parents allow me to use the car.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists allow v. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /əˈlaʊ/ and the meaning 'give permission' or 'make possible', but its Learner's Dictionary labels the permission sense B1. The project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example uses the pattern allow somebody to do something.

example_en: I almost missed the train.
example_uk: Я мало не запізнився на потяг.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists almost adv. at A2. Cambridge Learner's Dictionary confirms UK pronunciation /ˈɔːlməʊst/ and the meaning 'very close to happening but not happening'. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate this meaning.

example_en: She lives alone.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists alone adj. and adv. at A2. Cambridge Learner's Dictionary confirms UK pronunciation /əˈləʊn/ and the meaning 'without other people'. The example and Ukrainian translation are natural. As an adjective, alone normally follows a linking verb and does not come directly before a noun.

example_en: We walked along the river.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists along prep. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /əˈlɒŋ/ and labels the meaning 'from one part of a road, river, etc. to another' A2. Other senses and adverbial uses may have higher CEFR levels. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the A2 prepositional sense.

example_en: I've already finished my homework.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists already adv. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /ɔːlˈred.i/ and the A2 meaning 'before the present time'. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate an action completed before now.

example_en: We need to find an alternative.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists alternative n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /ɒlˈtɜː.nə.tɪv/ for the noun but labels the noun B2; the project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the noun meaning 'another possibility or choice'.

example_en: Although it was cold, we went for a walk.
example_uk: Хоча було холодно, ми пішли на прогулянку.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists although conj. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ɔːlˈðəʊ/ and the conjunction meaning 'despite the fact that', but labels the core sense B1. The project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example and Ukrainian translation correctly show contrast.

example_en: She was happy to be among friends.
example_uk: Вона була рада бути серед друзів.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists among prep. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈmʌŋ/ and labels the sense 'included as part of a group' A2; the separate sense 'in the middle of or surrounded by' is B1. The example illustrates the A2 group-membership sense.

example_en: We need a large amount of water.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists amount n. at A2 (the verb is B2). Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈmaʊnt/ and the noun meaning a quantity, but labels the main noun sense B1. The project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example correctly uses amount with an uncountable noun.

example_en: They visited an ancient castle.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists ancient adj. at A2. Cambridge confirms the UK pronunciation /ˈeɪnʃənt/ and the meaning 'from a long time ago'. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the historical-age sense.

example_en: He hurt his ankle while playing football.
example_uk: Він травмував щиколотку під час гри у футбол.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists ankle n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /ˈæŋ.kəl/ and defines the ankle as the joint connecting the foot and leg. The example and Ukrainian translation match this body-part meaning.

example_en: I can't run any faster.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists any adv. at A2. Cambridge Learner's Dictionary gives UK strong /ˈeni/, weak /əni/ and labels the adverbial intensifier before comparatives B1. The project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example illustrates this adverbial use, not the A1 determiner/pronoun uses.

example_en: Did anybody call me?
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists anybody pron. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /ˈen.iˌbɒd.i/ and the use of anybody in questions and negative sentences to mean any person. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate a question.

example_en: I don't work there any more.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists any more adv. at A2. Cambridge British Grammar confirms the two-word British spelling and the adverbial meaning 'no longer'; the one-word form anymore is mainly American. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate an action that has stopped.

ukrainian_translation: у будь-якому разі; все одно; зрештою
example_en: It was raining, but we went out anyway.
example_uk: Йшов дощ, але ми все одно вийшли.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists anyway adv. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /ˈen.i.weɪ/ and A2 uses meaning 'whatever else is happening' and to return to or change a topic. The example illustrates the concessive 'in spite of that' use.

example_en: You can sit anywhere.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists anywhere adv. and pron. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /ˈen.i.weə(r)/ and A2 meanings 'in, to, or at any place'. The broad non-rhotic IPA omits optional post-vocalic /r/. The example illustrates the adverbial place use.

example_en: I use an app to learn English.
example_uk: Я використовую застосунок, щоб вивчати англійську.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists app n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /æp/. The noun means a computer program, especially one used on a phone or tablet. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the mobile-application sense.

example_en: A message appeared on the screen.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists appear v. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈpɪə(r)/, represented here in broad non-rhotic IPA without post-vocalic /r/. Cambridge labels the common 'start to be seen' sense B1; the project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example illustrates something becoming visible.

example_en: The building has a modern appearance.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists appearance n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈpɪə.rəns/; the non-rhotic broad form is /əˈpɪərəns/. The example uses the meaning 'the way something looks'. Other noun senses, such as a public performance or court appearance, are distinct. The Ukrainian translation matches the visual sense.

example_en: I want to apply for this job.
example_uk: Я хочу подати заявку на цю роботу.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists apply v. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈplaɪ/. The example illustrates the formal-request pattern 'apply for a job'. Cambridge labels this sense B1; the project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The Ukrainian translation is accurate.

example_en: The architect designed our new house.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists architect n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈɑː.kɪ.tekt/. Cambridge labels the profession sense B1; the project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the profession.

example_en: I like the architecture of this city.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists architecture n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈɑː.kɪ.tek.tʃə(r)/, represented in broad non-rhotic IPA without post-vocalic /r/. Cambridge labels the art and practice of designing buildings B1; the project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example illustrates the field/style of buildings.

example_en: They often argue about money.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists argue v. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈɑːɡ.juː/. Cambridge labels the common disagreement sense B1; the project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate disagreement.

example_en: We had an argument yesterday.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists argument n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈɑːɡ.jə.mənt/. Cambridge labels the disagreement sense B1; the project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example uses the countable sense 'a disagreement' and the Ukrainian translation conveys the event naturally.

example_en: He joined the army at eighteen.
example_uk: У вісімнадцять років він вступив до армії.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists army n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈɑː.mi/. Cambridge labels the country's military force sense B1; the project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate joining the armed forces.

example_en: I'll arrange a meeting for Monday.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists arrange v. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈreɪndʒ/. Cambridge labels the planning/organising sense B1; the project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records the discrepancy. The example uses the natural collocation 'arrange a meeting'.

example_en: We made an arrangement to meet at six.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists arrangement n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈreɪndʒ.mənt/ but labels the common plan/agreement noun sense B1. The project follows Oxford for CEFR placement and records this discrepancy. The example illustrates an agreement or plan; the Ukrainian translation is natural.

example_en: She works as a teacher.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists as adv. and conj. at A2; its preposition use is separately A1. Cambridge confirms UK weak-form pronunciation /əz/ (strong form /æz/) and the conjunction/adverb uses. The example illustrates the role/identity pattern 'work as'. This entry does not cover the A1 prepositional use.

example_en: The baby is asleep.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists asleep adj. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈsliːp/ and the meaning 'sleeping'. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the predicative adjective; asleep is not normally used directly before a noun.

example_en: Ask the shop assistant for help.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists assistant n. and adj. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈsɪs.tənt/ and the noun meaning a person who helps. The example illustrates the shop-assistant compound. The adjective use means helping or supporting and is a separate grammatical use.

example_en: The athlete trains every morning.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists athlete n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈæθ.liːt/ and defines an athlete as a person who is very good at sports or competes in sports events. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate this meaning.

example_en: The town came under attack.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists attack n. and v. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈtæk/ and the noun sense of a violent or forceful attempt to hurt or damage. The example illustrates the noun; the verb has the corresponding action meaning.

example_en: I attend English classes twice a week.
example_uk: Я відвідую заняття з англійської двічі на тиждень.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists attend v. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈtend/ and the meaning 'go to an event, place or meeting'. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate attending classes.

example_en: Please pay attention to the instructions.
example_uk: Будь ласка, зверніть увагу на інструкції.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists attention n. and exclamation at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈtenʃ.ən/ and the noun meaning the act of watching, listening or thinking carefully. The example uses the collocation 'pay attention'. The exclamation is a separate use, as in 'Attention, please!'.

example_en: The house has an attractive garden.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists attractive adj. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈtræk.tɪv/ and meanings including pleasant to look at or interesting. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate visual appeal.

example_en: The audience clapped at the end of the show.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists audience n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈɔː.di.əns/ and defines audience as the group of people watching or listening to a performance, speech or broadcast. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate this collective noun.

example_en: Who is the author of this book?
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists author n. at A2. Cambridge gives UK /ˈɔː.θə(r)/; the broad non-rhotic form is /ˈɔːθə/. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the person who wrote the book.

example_en: Is this seat available?
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists available adj. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /əˈveɪ.lə.bəl/ and the meaning 'able to be used or obtained'. The example illustrates something that is free to use.

example_en: The average age of the students is twenty.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists average adj. and n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /ˈæv.ər.ɪdʒ/. This record covers the common adjective meaning 'typical or usual' and the related noun meaning a usual or typical amount; both are listed at A2 by Oxford. The example illustrates the adjective use.

example_en: Try to avoid making the same mistake.
example_uk: Намагайся не повторювати ту саму помилку.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists avoid v. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /əˈvɔɪd/ and the meaning 'stay away from someone or something, or prevent something from happening'. The example uses the pattern avoid + -ing.

example_en: She won an award for her work.
example_uk: Вона отримала нагороду за свою роботу.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists award n. at A2; the verb is separately classified B1. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /əˈwɔːd/. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate a prize given for achievement.

example_en: The weather was awful yesterday.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists awful adj. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈɔː.fəl/ and labels the meaning 'extremely bad or unpleasant' A2. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate this sense, not the separate B2 intensifier use.

example_en: We use the back door.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists back adj. at A2; the noun and adverb are A1, and the verb is B2. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /bæk/. This record is specifically the adjective meaning at or near the rear of something. The example illustrates the adjective modifying door.

example_en: The mountains form a beautiful background.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists background n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈbæk.ɡraʊnd/ and meanings including the area behind the main subject of a picture or view, and a person's past or experience. The example illustrates the visual-background sense.

example_en: He was badly hurt in the accident.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists badly adv. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈbæd.li/ and meanings including 'in a severe or harmful way' and 'not well'. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the severity meaning.

example_en: We met at a bar near the station.
example_uk: Ми зустрілися в барі біля вокзалу.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists bar n. at A2; the verb is B2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /bɑː/ and the place sense of a bar where drinks are served. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate this noun sense.

example_en: Baseball is popular in the United States.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists baseball n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈbeɪs.bɔːl/ and defines it as a game played with a bat and ball by two teams. The example illustrates the sport.

example_en: The company is based in London.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists based adj. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /beɪst/ and the adjective use in patterns such as be based in a place. The example and translation illustrate the location of an organisation.

example_en: We play basketball at school.
example_uk: Ми граємо в баскетбол у школі.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists basketball n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈbɑː.skɪt.bɔːl/ and defines the sport. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the activity.

example_en: Add a few beans to the soup.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists bean n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /biːn/ and the meaning of an edible seed from a plant. The example and translation illustrate the food sense.

example_en: We saw a bear in the forest.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists bear (animal) n. at A2; the verb meaning 'carry/deal with' is B2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /beə(r)/, represented in broad non-rhotic IPA without post-vocalic /r/. The example illustrates the animal sense.

example_en: Our team beat the champions.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists beat v. at A2; the noun is B2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /biːt/ and the verb meaning 'defeat someone in a game or competition'. The example illustrates this sense.

example_en: We had beef and vegetables for dinner.
example_uk: На вечерю ми їли яловичину з овочами.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists beef n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /biːf/ and defines beef as meat from a cow. The example and Ukrainian translation illustrate the food sense.

example_en: Wash your hands before you eat.
example_uk: Помий руки перед тим, як їсти.
notes: Oxford 3000 lists before conj. at A2; its preposition use is A1. Cambridge British Grammar confirms before can introduce a clause and that the present simple is used for future reference. UK non-rhotic IPA is /bɪˈfɔː/. The example illustrates the conjunction.

example_en: I've seen this film before.
example_uk: Я вже бачив цей фільм раніше.
notes: Oxford 3000 lists before adv. at A2; its preposition use is A1. Cambridge confirms UK pronunciation /bɪˈfɔː(r)/ and the adverbial meaning 'at an earlier time'. The example and translation illustrate this use.

example_en: The children behaved well at the party.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists behave v. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /bɪˈheɪv/ and the meaning 'act in a particular way'. The example and translation illustrate conduct.

example_en: His behaviour was very polite.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists behaviour n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /bɪˈheɪ.vjə(r)/, represented in broad non-rhotic IPA without post-vocalic /r/. The example and translation illustrate the way someone acts.

example_en: This bag belongs to my sister.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists belong v. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /bɪˈlɒŋ/ and the sense of being someone's property or being in the right place. The example illustrates ownership and the pattern belong to.

example_en: He wears a black leather belt.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists belt n. at A2. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /belt/ and the meaning of a strip worn around the waist. The example and translation illustrate the clothing accessory.

example_en: One benefit of exercise is better sleep.
example_uk: Одна з переваг фізичних вправ — кращий сон.
notes: Oxford 3000 by CEFR level lists benefit n. at A2; the verb is B1. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /ˈben.ɪ.fɪt/ and the noun meaning a helpful or good effect. The example illustrates this sense.

example_en: Which team played best?
notes: Oxford 3000 lists best adv. at A2; the adjective is A1. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /best/ and the superlative adverb meaning 'in the most successful or suitable way'. The example illustrates the adverbial use.

ukrainian_translation: найкраще; найкраща частина; найкраще з можливого
example_en: We always want the best for our children.
example_uk: Ми завжди хочемо найкращого для наших дітей.
notes: Oxford 3000 lists best n. at A2; the adjective is A1. Cambridge confirms UK IPA /best/ and noun uses meaning the most excellent person or thing, or the best part. The example illustrates 'the best' as a noun phrase.

example_en: She can speak English better now.
